What is supposed to the be the ROI for marketing when it comes to AI adoption?

That question is harder to answer than it might sound when you have to boil it down to a sentence.

For instance, the value return for Sales is simple:  if they go from spending 40% of their time talking to buyers and customers to 70% of their time, that's a very clear return AI enables for them.

For Product and Engineering, if they are shipping code 40% faster with 20% fewer bugs making it to live production, the return on AI for them is very clear.

For Marketing, what is that supposed to be? It's less clear cut where AI is going to actually help marketing in the long run. Because “what is the job of marketing” is rarely well defined by the people hiring them.

Right now we have defaulted into talking about it in terms of speed. We ship X amount of content faster. We get reports daily, not weekly, and in less time. Creating target lists and personalizing them happens faster than it ever could before.

But is it making the profession more effective? Is your traffic and AEO mentions going up because you're publishing faster? Are your reports making your iterations better because you get data that is significant enough to act on? Is all that extra personalization driving more meetings via inbound?

That's a question that very few marketers want to have honest conversations  on LinkedIn about.

Because with the drive towards AI adoption has made marketing a Temu version of itself, where everything tends to look like a cheap imitation of the next. 

Your Founder brand posts all sounds the same. Your automated comments are training your actual writing style. How much can your audience believe your testimonial videos - are they a real person?

Marketing at its core still needs authenticity and story to be memorable. That's why even before AI, crappy cold emails got ignored. Milquetoast ebook lead gen never drove a deal. And boring, undifferentiated positioning and messaging never got a middling company to a new level.

AI can do a lot of great things to help you in your work, but its never going to replace your creativity and your intuition. You have to own that. 

So what is the return on AI supposed to be for marketers? Can you condense it to a simple statement?

My wife is studying to become a certified toxicologist and wants to be able to practice the exam whenever she can.

Problem:  There is no way to take a DABT practice exam where the questions are hard enough to mimic the actual test.

Solution: Vibe code it myself with AI. Call it Project Francesca.

And that's exactly what I did and got a working prototype going in 2 weeks:

➡️ A 1000 question bank covering over 6000 pages of exam material
➡️ Randomized 160 question generator
➡️ Reference text for every question after she answers
➡️ 4 hour timer

Doing this project helped me realize a few things with AI and vibe coding:

First is that all the language we use to describe making these assets are designed to make you feel dumb. I didn't know what I was doing when I made this. I spoke to the LLM and it did it. The hardest part was getting the exam material organized and getting the tools I had never used before setup and talking:  Cursor, Vercel, Github, and Codex early on to get a prototype.

Second, I have way more respect for engineers than I did before. Your wife asking you to make tweaks and then expecting them immediately while you work with a developer stack to fix things was a workflow I had never experienced before. 

You can see why it takes time to ship things. The disconnect between a product request (what my wife was dictating to me) and actually executing on it is far.

Third is, we used to say ideas were cheap and execution is what matters. More than ever no I feel the opposite. The execution is actually now what's cheap, and the idea is what matters. 

You need a legit idea that helps somebody do something they couldn't otherwise do.

It helps immensely to have a real subject matter expert working alongside you. I have no idea how easy or hard the questions I was generating are. I can't immediately tell if they were correct. I can't totally discern how closely the questions reflect a certification exam.

But my wife, PhD and multi-year biotech professional, knows. So she was my eyes and ears while I brainstormed how to make her feedbacks happen.

The end result is hardly the end result. She is going to take a week to do a few practice exams, give me feedback, we will create a PRD, and I will continue to refine this for her all the way leading up to her exam in October.

But being able to make something for someone you love so they can get to their next level professionally is an energy that is lightning in a bottle. The type of forcing function that got me into doing something I had been intrigued to try for months. 

I could not dream about doing something like this 18 months ago. The world moves very fast.

Happy Father's Day, dad. Thanks for showing me what being there for your family is all about.

You can think AI is a completely transformative technology that will fundamentally change the way we work and believe the current cycle is a bubble destined to burst.

These two positions do not need to be exclusive one another.

In a lot of ways, the first thing has already happened. Anyone not using AI right now and increasing adoption of it is probably setting themselves up for future irrelevancy.

But that does not mean the current levels for AI investment are not way above their skis and likely to cause sizable economic downside in the short term.

There are good parallels between the current AI infrastructure investment and the railroad land grant expansions of the 1800s. The cost is being shouldered disproportionately by those not benefiting much from the technology.

We are being subsidized right now to learn, share, and be the product for AI at the moment. This because for all of the adoption and spend, the financial impact right now is relatively low.

And the cost of using AI is destined to rise as the price of it goes up with it.

AI infrastructure right now is built with private capital and public subsidies as companies state shop for the best tax breaks for data centers. The returns will come to a small number of companies and high-skill workers, while the grid and tax costs are likely to fall on the households least likely to ever use the compute. I am watching this play out right now in Western Maryland as citizens are lining up to sign petitions to put these kinds of measures on the ballot - mostly to say they do not want it.

That's in many ways the railroad land grant model with better PR.

What's most wild when looking at these two bubbles comparatively is the timeline. The railroad expansion and crashes happened over 50 years with 2 distinct crashes.

We call this socializing the losses and privatizing the gains. 

The current AI infrastructure trajectory has this happening 5 times faster and with far less clear visibility because ROI is largely self-reported.

So yes, embrace this change. Get familiar with this technology. Comment on these weak Claude Skill templates and start to figure out how to use them for your business.

Make yourself more attractive to employers and more indispensable to your senior leadership.

But don't think this bill isn't coming due at some point sooner rather than later.

People love to push measurement in places it does not belong.

Probably nowhere is that more constant than when people try to measure their brand investments.

It's fairly straightforward to measure brand if you understand the limits of measuring it and apply it correctly. And of course, don't treat it and measure it like performance marketing because it doesn't behave that way.

Brand requires in the short term looking at exposed audience against unexposed audiences against your performance marketing efforts.

So if you have a TAL of 2K accounts: 

➡️ Run brand advertising to 1K of those accounts (all relevant personas) 
➡️ Run direct response response to all 2K of those account (ads, email, calls)
➡️ Look at the difference down funnel of the exposed and unexposed cohort

That's the simplest way to go about doing brand advertising and answering:  what is it giving us compared to if we didn't do it at all?

If it's not giving you an incremental return against the unexposed account list, now you can action your messaging, targeting, creative / channel choices, etc.

There are slews of ways to look at it at higher levels and over longer time horizons, but the simplest way to get a brand campaign effort off the ground for advertising is to design it simple, make what you want to affect clear, and work with your leadership team to make the effectiveness unmistakable.

AI might not be the switching trigger you think it is.

Everyone here believes that their AI capability is the single common factor that would compel a company to leave their incumbent or choose you instead.

But have you actually asked your target customer if that's the case?

Because we often believe that simply existing as a company and being a great product is reason enough for people to want to buy us, we sometimes grossly underestimate the type of concerns buyers bring to a sales process that you need to proactively prepared to answer, preferrably before they enter a sales process.

For instance, having a best-in-class AI first solution is going to draw the interest of lots of early adopters. 

But once that market dries up and you have to expand to a more grounded audience, you are going to run into pushbacks you will need to answer for in your positioning, product, and onboarding like:

- Is the AI built-in to the product or bolted on?
- Is it going to be internal or external facing?
- What legal exposure exists from your AI feature?
-  How does it deal with regulatory constraints?

AI is a retention and a perception tool. Buyers need to trust how it works and the constraints built into it before they get too excited about the capabilities it can provide.

At least once you get outside the gleeful applications of the sales and martech space.

And that doesn't even factor in how its priced into the solution.

So while there are a lot of pockets on LinkedIn and on X simply saying 'Go Go Go' with regard to AI adoption and infusing it into your tech, skipping the fundamental parts of discovery that make that AI native solution durable and scalable outside the early adopter market is a long term risk in a booming but still fragile market.

Move fast but learn and iterate even faster.

Before marketers learn AI, or the language of the boardroom, or purpose, or storytelling, or any of the other things we keep telling them they need to master, many of them need to learn something more basic. They need to learn marketing.

That's Mark Ritson's read on the state of the marketing profession and I am struggling to disagree with the assessment.

This is off an Ipsos survey of 1,226 marketers from the United States, Canada, and Britain that showed only 35% of marketers - 35% (!!!!!) - could pass a 10 question foundational benchmark of marketing fundamentals.

We are talking basic questions like what a real market research method is, what segmentation / targeting / positioning is, and if they could name the 4Ps. 

Name them.

Even more curious is the cognitive dissonance of the profession. While only 35% could pass this test, most rate their skills very highly.

And why wouldn't they - we are in an era where people are more impressed by Gizmo Marketing than by doing actual marketing.

Which is why you see so many proudly talk about how formal marketing training creates a deficit, is irrelevant, or somehow holds your career back.

These are many of the same marketers who can only measure their success through direct attribution or insist every single activity done directly impact a revenue outcome within a quarter's time else it "not count".

We are moving into a time where the pace of play is faster than ever, which makes the fundamentals and the foundations more important than ever.

So while we zoom past formal training and declare marketing as only Promotion, remember the job is so much more than being a servant to other departments and ceding your ability to impact the outcomes.
